rv.q: A disjointed evening begins to generate an authentic sense of the tragic.

They could do this show in a wind tunnel. What’s more, Lear goes from proud king to raging outcast to whimpering disaster area in two hours flat. That’s a good percentage off the running time of rival 21st-century Lears Ian McKellen, Antony Sher, Glenda Jackson, Derek Jacobi, Jonathan Pryce or Simon Russell Beale.
As a production it is packed with action and deft in its fight scenes, but remains rather flat, and perhaps unwilling to plumb this play's tragic depths.
This Lear feels like a dress rehearsal for Branagh – a much grander outing at some later point is surely in the works.
Peel away the brutal pruning of the text, and casting that is blind to age, ethnicity and gender, and this is a solidly old-fashioned staging.
Yet every time Branagh returns to the stage, he insists upon directing himself rather than entrusting the task to someone with an outside perspective.

At one point, Branagh literally stands in the way of Jessica Revell as she struggles to untangle the painfully convoluted gags of Lear's beloved Fool. But she's also tasked with playing Lear's good daughter Cordelia, in whom Branagh shows little interest.

It is set in ancient Britain (a nod, perhaps, to Branagh’s great hero Laurence Olivier, who did a druid-style version of the play on TV 40 years ago) with the cast in Game Of Thrones-style wolfskins, big sticks instead of swords and everyone needing a good wash. On the evidence here, Branagh also needs a good director.

Matter?” Is this ancient Britspeak? The effect is not quite pronounced enough to suggest a distinctive dialect but is more than sufficient to mangle the sense of the verse, with subjects and verbs waving at each other across the gulf of a pause.
Confused in concept and clumsy in execution, it manages to be at once overblown and insubstantial.
This is an attractively, if unevenly, packaged version 'King Lear'.
It feels like a trial run and that Branagh's Lear is still to come.
Their characters and lines are cut, and they race through their speeches, skating gamely along the surface but never penetrating the depths beneath.
Branagh's vision is undeniably there, but the execution lacks directorial precision.
A fantastic take on a new facet of a timeless classic.

cn.t: Branagh's "King Lear" earns mostly positive reviews for its compelling staging and powerful moments, though some critics find the production uneven. Strong performances and simple yet effective design elevate this bleak, human take on Shakespeare's tragedy.
